headline: BJP MP calls for 'reclaiming' Noakhali, Ctg Port, Sylhet from Bangladesh, citing Partition-era claims
summary: Nishikant Dubey, an Indian lawmaker, claimed these territories were handed to East Pakistan during Partition without the Tripura kingdom ruler's consent, blaming India's first PM Jawaharlal Nehru.
details: BJP lawmaker Nishikant Dubey has called for India to "reclaim" Noakhali, Chittagong Port, and Sylhet from Bangladesh. He made these remarks on Friday, blaming India's first prime minister Jawaharlal Nehru for the decision.

Dubey claimed the territories were handed over to East Pakistan during Partition without the consent of the ruler of the erstwhile Tripura kingdom, according to The Hindu. He alleged Nehru wanted the Muslim League's support in the interim government formed in 1946.

"My view is that the time has come not just to reclaim Pakistan-occupied Kashmir from Pakistan. It is also time to reclaim the territories that Nehru ji forcibly handed over, whether it is Noakhali, Chittagong Port or Sylhet," Dubey told Indian news agency ANI.

According to The Hindu, Dubey's remarks received backing from Pradyot Manikya, a descendant of Tripura's erstwhile royal family and head of the Tipra Motha party. Manikya stated that huge parts of the erstwhile Tripura Kingdom were ceded to East Pakistan without his grandmother's knowledge during Partition.

Manikya also linked the loss of Chattogram to the northeastern Indian region's lack of direct access to the sea. He argued that the decision had left the region geographically constrained, impacting its development.

Dubey further claimed that Bir Bikram Kishore Manikya, the then king of Tripura, had opposed the interim government's decision on the future of Noakhali, Sylhet, and Chattogram. The king reportedly challenged Nehru, stating, "This is my kingdom. I will decide whether it remains part of India, Pakistan or becomes an independent state."

headline: Bangladesh LPG prices soar 52% since February, costing 30-45% more than neighbors
summary: Official retail LPG prices in Bangladesh have surged by nearly 52% since February, making them 30-45% higher than published rates in Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Nepal. This increase is largely due to disrupted Middle Eastern supplies and higher freight costs from
details: Consumers in Bangladesh are paying around 30 to 45 percent more for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) than the official retail rates in Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Nepal. The official retail price of LPG in Bangladesh has surged by nearly 52 percent since February.

This sharp increase is attributed to the disruption of Middle Eastern supplies, which forced importers to seek more distant sources like the US. This shift has significantly pushed up freight costs and premiums for securing cargoes.

The price per kilogram rose from Tk 113 in February to Tk 171.68 in November. Over the same period, official retail prices in Pakistan rose by 34 percent, Sri Lanka by 12 percent, and Nepal by 6 percent.

At the November rate, LPG cost approximately Tk 132 per kg in Pakistan, Tk 130 in Sri Lanka, and Tk 119 in Nepal based on published prices. However, market prices in Pakistan are reportedly much higher than official rates.

India's household consumers pay around Tk 87 per kg, but this rate is not directly comparable due to government subsidies. Commercial LPG in Delhi, however, costs around Tk 194 per kg, exceeding Bangladesh's regulated retail price.

Bangladesh faces structural disadvantages, including its relatively small purchasing volume and heavy dependence on spot market purchases. Additionally, there's an extra cost for transferring LPG from large mother vessels to smaller ones before bringing it ashore.

Indian buyers can purchase around 1 lakh tonnes in a single vessel, while Bangladeshi companies typically buy much smaller quantities. This gives larger buyers stronger bargaining power in the international market.

The US share of Bangladesh's LPG imports dramatically increased from 27.4 percent in September 2022 to 85 percent in September this year. This shift came after the conflict in the Middle East and restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Shipments from the US Gulf take 40 to 45 days to reach Bangladesh, compared to roughly two weeks from Middle Eastern suppliers. Freight costs for US-origin cargoes have also surged from about $82 per tonne before the conflict to as much as $250 per tonne.
